title: Austria-Hungary
titleline: Austria-Hungary - The History Web
para1: Austria-Hungary. Austria-Hungary was born of defeat: after Prussia crushed Austria in 1866, the Habsburgs made their peace with the Hungarians in the Compromise of 1867, transforming the Austrian Empire into a dual monarchy - two largely self-governing states, Cisleithania and Transleithania, sharing one monarch who was both Emperor of Austria and Apostolic King of Hungary. It was the last phase in the constitutional evolution of the Habsburg monarchy, following Hungary's wars of independence against Habsburg rule, above all the revolution of 1848-1849.
para2: Under the long reign of Franz Joseph (1867-1916), the dual monarchy was one of Europe's great powers and one of its strangest states: a dozen nations - Germans, Hungarians, Czechs, Slovaks, Poles, Ukrainians, Romanians, Croats, Serbs, Slovenes, Italians - under one crown, with a dazzling imperial capital in Vienna and a proud partner capital in Budapest. It was the second-largest country in Europe by area and the third-most populous, and it built the fourth-largest machine-building industry in the world.
para3: The dual structure had been born in failure: in 1848 the Hungarians' revolution for independence was crushed by the Austrian army with Russian help, and absolutist rule from Vienna only deepened the resentment that the 1867 Compromise was designed to end. The national tensions that made the monarchy colorful also made it fragile. When the heir, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, was assassinated at Sarajevo on 28 June 1914, the July Crisis ended with Austria-Hungary's declaration of war on Serbia on 28 July - the fuse of the First World War, in which the dual monarchy fought as one of the Central Powers, a war it would not survive.
para4: Defeat and nationalist revolution dissolved the empire even before the armistice: Hungary terminated the union in October 1918, and the armistice of Villa Giusti followed on 3 November. From its lands rose Austria, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, and Yugoslavia, with territories ceded to Poland, Romania, and Italy - the map of Central Europe for the century to come.

title: The Dutch Republic / Kingdom of the Netherlands
titleline: The Dutch Republic / Kingdom of the Netherlands - The History Web
para1: The Dutch Republic and the Kingdom of the Netherlands. The Dutch Republic was born in revolt: on 26 July 1581 the northern Netherlands renounced their Spanish king in the Act of Abjuration, and the young republic fought on for nearly seventy years before Spain accepted the Peace of Munster in 1648. The improbable little state of merchants and sailors then produced the Dutch Golden Age: Amsterdam became the world's commercial and financial capital, and the Dutch East India Company (VOC) and West India Company (GWC) made the republic a global trading empire that let it compete militarily with far larger states.
para2: The 17th-century republic was a marvel: more tolerant of different religions and ideas than any contemporary state, it drew in refugees - Iberian Jews, Huguenots, English Dissenters, even the Pilgrim Fathers - and Amsterdam became the hub of world trade. Artists flourished - Rembrandt, Vermeer - and scientists too: Grotius, Huygens, and Leeuwenhoek. Its unique government, a republic of provinces led by its stadtholders, balanced merchant oligarchy and the House of Orange, and it fought four Anglo-Dutch Wars against its greatest rival.
para3: The 18th century brought relative decline as Britain and France outgrew it; in 1795 the republic fell to revolutionary France in the Batavian Revolution. After Napoleon's defeat, the Congress of Vienna created the United Kingdom of the Netherlands, merging the Dutch Republic's lands with the Austrian Netherlands under King William I of Orange. The union lasted only fifteen years: the Belgian Revolution of 1830 split the south away.
para4: The reduced Kingdom of the Netherlands built a prosperous trading state, and today it remains a constitutional monarchy and one of the world's great trading nations: the small country that once ran the world's commerce.

title: The French Revolution & Napoleonic France
titleline: The French Revolution & Napoleonic France - The History Web
para1: The French Revolution and Napoleonic France. In May 1789, a bankrupt French monarchy summoned the Estates General for the first time since 1614. The representatives of the Third Estate broke away and declared themselves a National Assembly; on 14 July Paris stormed the Bastille. Within weeks the Assembly had abolished feudalism, taken control of the Catholic Church, and issued the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen - the charter of liberal democracy.
para2: The revolution radicalized: the monarchy fell, the First Republic was proclaimed in September 1792, and Louis XVI was executed. From June 1793 power passed to the Jacobin-dominated Committee of Public Safety under Maximilien Robespierre: the Reign of Terror sent some 16,000 people to execution before Robespierre himself fell in July 1794. The unstable Directory that followed (1795) lasted until 9 November 1799, when General Napoleon Bonaparte seized power in the Coup of 18 Brumaire and made himself First Consul.
para3: Napoleon consolidated the revolution's gains - and buried its republic. In December 1804 he crowned himself Emperor of the French, and for a decade his armies dominated Europe: Austerlitz in 1805 shattered the Third Coalition and dissolved the Holy Roman Empire, Jena-Auerstedt crushed Prussia in 1806, and his Napoleonic Code, public education, and equality before the law reshaped France and the lands he conquered - though he also abolished the free press and reinstated slavery in the colonies. The invasion of Russia in 1812 ended in catastrophic retreat; defeated and exiled to Elba in 1814, he escaped, ruled again for the Hundred Days, and met final defeat at Waterloo in June 1815, dying on Saint Helena in 1821.
para4: The revolution and Napoleon together remade the world: they spread the ideas of equality before the law, popular sovereignty, and nationalism across Europe, redrew the continent's map, and established the model of the modern centralized state - while the wars that devastated Europe and Napoleon's mixed record on civil rights keep his legacy contested. France's own upheavals continued through the revolutions of 1830 and 1848.

title: The German Empire
titleline: The German Empire - The History Web
para1: The German Empire. The German Empire - the Second Reich - was proclaimed in 1871 after the wars of unification, and lasted until the revolution of November 1918. It was a federation of 25 states: four constituent kingdoms, six grand duchies, duchies, principalities, and three free Hanseatic cities, each keeping its own nobility - plus the imperial territory of Alsace-Lorraine. But one state towered over the rest: Prussia held two-thirds of the empire's people and land, and the King of Prussia was, constitutionally, the German Emperor.
para2: The empire's first chancellor, Otto von Bismarck (1871-1890), dominated its first two decades: under Kaiser Wilhelm I he built the alliance system that kept Europe's peace and made Germany the leading power on the continent. The economy boomed: by 1913 Germany was the largest economy in continental Europe and the third largest in the world, with Europe's most extensive rail network and the world's strongest army - and a navy that grew within a decade to second only to Britain's Royal Navy. German science led the world: a third of all Nobel Prizes went to German researchers.
para3: The accession of Wilhelm II (1888-1918) changed the tone: Bismarck was dismissed in 1890, and the young kaiser's assertive diplomacy, naval building, and pursuit of overseas colonies alarmed Germany's neighbors and helped set the stage for the First World War, which Germany entered on 1 August 1914.
para4: The war destroyed the empire. Four years of total war, blockade, and defeat brought revolution: on 3 November 1918 the German revolution began, and on 9 November Wilhelm II abdicated and the republic was proclaimed. The Second Reich, born in victory, died in defeat after 47 years - but the unified Germany it created remains the Germany of today.

title: The Habsburg Monarchy / Austrian Empire
titleline: The Habsburg Monarchy / Austrian Empire - The History Web
para1: The Habsburg Monarchy and Austrian Empire. The Habsburgs built the most durable great power of Central Europe. From 1526, when they acquired Bohemia and Hungary, their realm was a 'composite monarchy': a collection of kingdoms, duchies, and counties - the Archduchy of Austria proper, Inner Austria, and Further Austria - with only partial shared laws, united by the person of the monarch and the Habsburg court itself. Under Charles V (1519-1556) the house ruled half of Europe plus the Spanish Empire - and from 1438 to 1806 the Habsburgs almost continuously wore the crown of the Holy Roman Emperors, with their dynastic capital at Vienna.
para2: The Austrian Habsburgs became the shield of Central Europe against the Ottomans: the relief of Vienna in 1683 and the Treaty of Karlowitz (1699) pushed the frontier deep into Hungary. Bohemia became a hereditary Habsburg land after the Battle of White Mountain (1620), and Hungary after the reconquest of 1687. In the 18th century, Maria Theresa (1740-1780) and her son Joseph II (1780-1790) rebuilt the ramshackle inheritance into a governed, reformed state - while the family also briefly held the Austrian Netherlands and lands in Italy.
para3: In 1804, as the Holy Roman Empire crumbled, the Habsburg lands were unified as the Austrian Empire; after Napoleon's defeat it stood at the head of the conservative order in Europe, until the revolutions of 1848 shook it and the long reign of Franz Joseph (1848-1916) began. Defeated by Prussia in 1866, the empire compromised with Hungary in 1867, becoming Austria-Hungary.
para4: The multi-national monarchy could not survive the age of nationalism: in late 1918, facing defeat in the First World War, it disbanded as its peoples proclaimed their own states - German-Austria, Hungary, and the South Slavs. Six centuries of Habsburg rule ended in days, but the empire's cities, laws, and institutions still mark Central Europe.

title: The Italian City-States (Renaissance)
titleline: The Italian City-States (Renaissance) - The History Web
para1: The Italian City-States and the Renaissance. Between the 14th and 17th centuries, the small city-states of Italy produced the Renaissance - the 'rebirth' that carried Europe from the Middle Ages into the modern world. It began in Tuscany, centered on Florence, whose bankers financed Europe's monarchs and laid the groundwork of capitalism; it spread to Venice, whose fleets had traded with the East since the Crusades, and to Rome, largely rebuilt by Renaissance popes like Julius II and Leo X.
para2: The achievement was total: Dante, Petrarch, and Boccaccio had already re-founded literature in the 14th century; now came Leonardo, Michelangelo, Raphael, Botticelli, and Titian in art; Brunelleschi and Palladio in architecture; Machiavelli in politics; Palestrina in music and Monteverdi at the birth of opera; Galileo in science. Venice's Aldine Press pioneered portable printed books, and Florence's wool trade and Venice's arsenal - a vast shipyard mass-producing vessels for a fleet of thousands - showed the wealth behind the beauty.
para3: The city-states were also Europe's diplomatic laboratory, balanced against each other in the Peace of Lodi (1454-1494). But the Italian Wars (1494-1559) made the peninsula the battleground of France and Spain, and the Renaissance's political freedom died - even as its ideas spread north to set off the Northern Renaissance. Italian explorers sailing for foreign kings - Columbus for Spain, Vespucci for Portugal, Verrazzano for France, Cabot for England - ushered in the Age of Discovery.
para4: The Renaissance left Europe its modern face: banking and accounting, diplomacy, the printed book, the revival of Greek and Roman learning, and an ideal of human achievement that shaped the Scientific Revolution and the modern world. It was the work of a few small, quarrelsome, dazzling cities - the richest region in Europe, and for two centuries its cultural capital.

title: The Kingdom of Belgium
titleline: The Kingdom of Belgium - The History Web
para1: The Kingdom of Belgium. Belgium's lands were 'the battlefield of Europe' for centuries: part of the Burgundian Netherlands, then ruled by Habsburg Spain (1556-1714), the Austrian Habsburgs (1714-1794), and Revolutionary France (1794-1815), before the Congress of Vienna folded them into the United Kingdom of the Netherlands. The union failed fast: on 4 October 1830, after a revolution in Brussels, Belgium declared its independence.
para2: The new kingdom installed Leopold I as king on 21 July 1831 - now Belgium's National Day - as a neutral, officially French-speaking constitutional monarchy, and then industrialized with astonishing speed: Belgium was the first country in continental Europe to industrialize, and its coal, steel, and railways made it one of the wealthiest small states in the world.
para3: Under Leopold II the Berlin Conference of 1885 ceded the vast Congo Free State to the king as his private possession; the savage exploitation of the Congolese in the ivory and rubber trade became an international scandal - missionaries and consuls documented mutilations and mass death - and in 1908 the Belgian state took the colony over from its discredited owner. Then in August 1914 Germany invaded, and Belgium became the battlefield of Europe once more: nearly the whole country spent four years under occupation, while the Belgian army held a corner of Flanders behind the Yser and 'Brave Little Belgium' became an Allied watchword.
para4: The war's end transformed Belgian politics: in 1919 universal male suffrage replaced the old plural vote, breaking the Catholic party's long dominance, and the Flemish movement's demands for Dutch-language equality could no longer be ignored. Reconstruction rebuilt the devastated west, Belgium joined France in occupying the Ruhr in 1923 to force reparations, and the kingdom emerged from the ordeal industrial, enriched by empire, and wary - a small country whose old neutrality had died in 1914.

title: The Kingdom of France (Valois & Bourbon)
titleline: The Kingdom of France (Valois & Bourbon) - The History Web
para1: The Kingdom of France under the Valois and the Bourbons. When Charles IV died in 1328 without a male heir, the main Capetian line ended, and under Salic law the crown passed to his cousin Philip VI of Valois - the succession dispute that, combined with the quarrel over English-held Gascony, ignited the Hundred Years' War (1337-1453) between the Valois kings and the Plantagenet kings of England. The century brought devastating warfare, civil war between Armagnacs and Burgundians, and the Black Death, which arrived from Italy in 1348: France's population, some 18-20 million in 1328, had been cut by half or more 150 years later.
para2: Yet France emerged victorious from the war and then plunged into the Italian Wars (1494-1559), where Spain and the Holy Roman Empire checked its ambitions. Under Francis I, the Renaissance came to France - and so did centralization: his Ordinance of Villers-Cotterets (1539) made French the language of law and administration. The Reformation split the kingdom into the Wars of Religion (1562-1598) between the Catholic majority and the Huguenots, until Henry IV of Bourbon - a Protestant turned Catholic - restored peace.
para3: The Bourbon century made France the superpower of Europe. Centralized under the Ancien Regime, France built the second-largest colonial empire in the world - over 10 million square kilometers at its peak around 1680, centered on New France in North America - and from the reign of Louis XIV to Napoleon's defeat in 1815 it was the dominant power on the continent.
para4: But the cost of glory mounted: colonial wars with Britain stripped France of most of North America by 1763, and the expensive intervention that helped the United States win independence brought little gain. Bankruptcy summoned the Estates General in 1789 - and the Revolution abolished the monarchy in 1792, ending a kingdom that had ruled since 987. Restored briefly in 1814-1815 and again from 1815, it finally dissolved in 1848.

title: The Kingdom of Great Britain & the British Empire
titleline: The Kingdom of Great Britain & the British Empire - The History Web
para1: The Kingdom of Great Britain and the British Empire. On 1 May 1707 the Acts of Union joined England and Scotland into the Kingdom of Great Britain, with Queen Anne as its first monarch; in 1800 Ireland joined the union. The new state was soon the world's leading power: already dominant in North America after wars with the Dutch and the French, Britain became a major power in India after the East India Company's victory at Plassey in 1757.
para2: The loss of the American colonies by 1783 was only a pause: after the defeat of France in the Napoleonic Wars (1803-1815), Britain emerged as the principal naval and imperial power of the 19th century. The century of relative peace it enforced became known as the Pax Britannica: Britain completed the conquest of India by 1818, forced trade concessions from China and Japan, joined the Scramble for Africa, and dominated world trade and finance.
para3: At its height in the 19th and early 20th centuries, the British Empire was the largest empire in history - by 1913 ruling 412 million people, 23 percent of the world's population, and by 1920 covering 35.5 million square kilometers, 24 percent of the Earth's land: 'the empire on which the sun never sets.' Its settler colonies grew into self-governing dominions, while its constitutional, legal, and linguistic legacy spread across the globe.
para4: The First World War tested the empire to its limit and changed it. The dominions - Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa - had sent armies and signed the peace as near-equals; Irish nationalists, after the Easter Rising of 1916 and a guerrilla war, won an Irish Free State in 1922; and in India the mass nationalism of Gandhi's non-cooperation movement challenged the Raj itself. Yet territorially the empire had never been larger, swelled by former Ottoman and German lands, and in 1924 the great Wembley exhibition paraded its products and peoples before millions of visitors. The Pax Britannica was over, but the empire on which the sun never set still spanned the globe.

title: The Kingdom of Greece
titleline: The Kingdom of Greece - The History Web
para1: The Kingdom of Greece. Modern Greece was born in the War of Independence: the first revolt rose in the Danubian principalities on 6 March 1821, and by the end of that month the Peloponnese was in open rebellion. After more than a decade of war, the Treaty of Constantinople (1832) formally recognized an independent Greece and established it as a monarchy under the Bavarian prince Otto of Wittelsbach, with its capital first at Nafplio, then from 1834 at Athens. Nearly four centuries of Ottoman rule had ended.
para2: The kingdom was born small, but it grew: Otto's absolutism was ended by the 3 September 1843 Revolution, which brought a constitution and universal male suffrage; a popular insurrection deposed Otto in 1862, and the Danish prince George I (1863-1913) began a fifty-year reign that brought the Ionian Islands from Britain in 1864 and the annexation of Thessaly in 1881. After the Goudi coup of 1909 brought Eleftherios Venizelos to power, Greece won the Balkan Wars of 1912-1913 - though King George himself was assassinated during the first of them.
para3: The First World War split the nation in the National Schism between King Constantine and Venizelos; Allied intervention brought Greece into the war and victory on the Macedonian Front. But the Asia Minor Campaign ended in disaster in 1922: the 11 September Revolution forced Constantine's abdication, the Treaty of Lausanne brought the population exchange between Greece and Turkey, and in 1924 the monarchy was abolished and the Second Hellenic Republic proclaimed.
para4: The republic proclaimed in March 1924 faced the enormous task of absorbing more than a million Greek refugees from Asia Minor into a country bankrupted by ten years of war. The monarchy was gone, Venizelos was the new republic's dominant figure, and the Asia Minor disaster - the 'Great Catastrophe' - had redrawn the Greek world: the centuries-old Greek communities of Anatolia were gone, and Greece's future now lay within the borders fixed at Lausanne.

title: The Kingdom of Prussia
titleline: The Kingdom of Prussia - The History Web
para1: The Kingdom of Prussia. The Kingdom of Prussia was the state that made Germany. It was born in 1701, when the Hohenzollern elector of Brandenburg - whose family had ruled those lands for centuries - crowned himself King Frederick I in Prussia on 18 January 1701. The kingdom took its name from the historical region of Prussia but was based in the Margraviate of Brandenburg, with its capital at Berlin.
para2: Through the 18th century Prussia rose from a scattered collection of territories into the most militarized and efficient of the German states: its population nearly tripled, from 2.2 million in 1740 to 5.8 million in 1786, as it expanded across northern Germany and held its own against the great powers of Europe. Crushed by Napoleon in 1806 and occupied as part of the French Continental System until 1813, Prussia reformed itself in defeat, returned to lead the wars of liberation, and emerged in 1815 as a leading power of the new German Confederation.
para3: In the 19th century, Prussia's destiny became Germany's: its industry, its army, and its statesmen drove the unification of Germany in 1871, and the King of Prussia became the German Emperor. Though only one of the empire's four kingdoms, Prussia held about two-thirds of its population and territory, and its minister-president was also the imperial chancellor: Prussia WAS imperial Germany.
para4: The kingdom died with the empire it created: in the revolution of November 1918 the monarchy fell, and Prussia became a Free State within the Weimar Republic. The state that had risen in three centuries from a Baltic duchy to the maker of Germany vanished into the greater Germany it had made.

title: The Kingdom of Romania
titleline: The Kingdom of Romania - The History Web
para1: The Kingdom of Romania. Romania was united before it was a kingdom: in 1859 Alexandru Ioan Cuza became prince of both Moldavia and Wallachia - the 'Little Union' - and in 1862 the two principalities formally merged as the Principality of Romania, with its capital at Bucharest, still nominally under Ottoman suzerainty. A Hohenzollern prince took the throne, and in the Russo-Turkish War of 1877-1878 - Romania's War of Independence - the country won full independence, trading southern Bessarabia for Northern Dobruja.
para2: In 1881 Romania was proclaimed a kingdom under Carol I (1881-1914), whose reign - the 'Old Kingdom' - brought stability, a constitution, railways, and the transformation of Bucharest into a European capital. The kingdom emerged from the First World War - which at one point drove the government from Bucharest to Iasi - into 'Greater Romania': Transylvania, Bessarabia, Bukovina, and the Banat joined the Old Kingdom after 1918, in the kingdom's greatest territorial extent.
para3: The kingdom emerged from the First World War - which at one point had driven the government from Bucharest to Iasi - into 'Greater Romania': Bessarabia voted union in March 1918, Bukovina in November, and on 1 December 1918 the great assembly at Alba Iulia proclaimed Transylvania's union with the kingdom, doubling Romania's territory and people. The peace settlement ratified the gains, and Ferdinand and Marie were crowned sovereigns of the enlarged kingdom in a spectacular ceremony at Alba Iulia in 1922.
para4: Building Greater Romania was the new kingdom's first work. The land reform of 1921 broke up the great estates for the peasant soldiers; the constitution of 1923 gave the enlarged state a centralized frame; and Romania anchored the Little Entente with Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia to guard the settlement against Hungary and Bulgaria. The kingdom now embraced many peoples - Hungarians, Germans, Jews, Ukrainians, and others alongside the Romanian majority - whose place in the national state the new order struggled to settle.

title: The Kingdom of Spain
titleline: The Kingdom of Spain - The History Web
para1: The Kingdom of Spain. Spain was born in 1469, when the marriage of Isabella I of Castile and Ferdinand II of Aragon joined the two great crowns of Iberia. In 1492 - the critical year of Spanish history - they conquered Granada, the last Muslim emirate in Spain, ending eight centuries of Al-Andalus; they expelled Spain's Jews; and they sponsored Christopher Columbus's first voyage to America. Within decades, the conquistadors had built a Spanish colonial empire among the largest in history, and Spain was the superpower of the age.
para2: The Habsburg century was Spain's Golden Age: under Charles I and his son Philip II, the empire reached its territorial and economic peak, Philip's palace-monastery at El Escorial the center of its power. But the strain showed: state bankruptcies, the destruction of the Armada, and the independence of the Northern Netherlands began the slow decline, continued through the Eighty Years' War and the Thirty Years' War. When the last Habsburg, Charles II, died heirless in 1700, the War of the Spanish Succession brought the French Bourbons to the throne - Philip V - and reforms under Charles III briefly revived the state.
para3: The 19th century brought collapse: Napoleon's invasion made Spain a French puppet state, and the wars of independence that followed cost Spain nearly all its American empire in the 1820s. A tumultuous century of pronunciamientos, Carlist wars and alternating liberal and conservative rule ended in the Disaster of 1898, when the United States destroyed two Spanish fleets and took Cuba, Puerto Rico and the Philippines - a humiliation that set off the national reckoning of the Generation of '98.
para4: Under the Restoration system two dynastic parties rotated power while local bosses fixed the elections, but social conflict mounted: anarchism spread among the workers, Catalonia demanded autonomy, and a grinding colonial war in Morocco climaxed in the massacre of the Spanish army at Annual in 1921, which destroyed the system's remaining credit. In September 1923, with the king's acquiescence, General Miguel Primo de Rivera seized power and dissolved the parliament, and by 1924 Spain was governed by a military directory ruling in Alfonso XIII's name.
source3label: Britannica: Philip II

title: The Ottoman Balkans
titleline: The Ottoman Balkans - The History Web
para1: The Ottoman Balkans. The Ottomans entered Europe in the mid-14th century, seizing Gallipoli in 1354 after an earthquake emptied the city - their base for the conquest of the Balkans. Adrianople fell in 1369, Thessalonica in 1387; the Serbian-led resistance broke at Kosovo, where Sultan Murad I himself was killed; and in 1453 Mehmed the Conqueror took Constantinople, ending the Byzantine Empire. Ottoman Europe - 'Rumelia' - was born.
para2: For two centuries the empire ruled the Balkans from the Danube to the Mediterranean: it fought Venice for four hundred years, suffering its great naval defeat at Lepanto in 1571 - then the largest naval battle in history - and its armies stood at the gates of Vienna. Only Corfu, of all the Greek islands, never fell to the Ottomans. The Balkan peoples - Greeks, Serbs, Bulgarians, Albanians, Romanians - lived under Ottoman rule for four or five centuries: Orthodox subjects of a Muslim sultan, their churches, languages, and memories preserved but their nations submerged.
para3: The 19th century tore the fabric: the Serbian uprising of 1804-1817 won autonomy, the Greek Revolution of 1821-1832 won independence, and the Romanian war of 1877-1878 - fought alongside Russia - freed the Danubian principalities. The great powers, especially Russia, pressed the empire in war after war - the Holy League's Great Turkish War (1683-1699) had already begun reversing its gains - and the Balkan states pressed it from within.
para4: The final retreat came in the Balkan Wars of 1912-1913, which drove the Ottomans almost out of Europe, and was sealed after the First World War by the Treaty of Sevres. Five centuries of Ottoman Europe ended; the borders, nations, and grievances it left behind still shape the Balkans today.

title: The Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth & its Partitions
titleline: The Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth & its Partitions - The History Web
para1: The Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth and its Partitions. The Commonwealth was born on 1 July 1569, when the Union of Lublin fused Poland and Lithuania - joined in dynastic union since 1385 - into a single state with its capital first at Krakow, then from 1596 at Warsaw. When the childless Sigismund II Augustus died in 1572, the Jagiellonian dynasty ended, and the Commonwealth became an elective monarchy: nobles or foreign dynasts elected to the throne for life.
para2: Its system - the Golden Liberty - was an early constitutional monarchy: the bicameral General Sejm held legislative power, the Henrician Articles bound the king, and the szlachta nobility, some 10 percent of the population, formed a kind of nobles' democracy. The Warsaw Confederation of 1573 guaranteed a religious tolerance remarkable for its age, and the Commonwealth's peoples - Poles, Lithuanians, Ruthenians, Germans, Jews - lived in unusual diversity.
para3: Its first royal election, in 1573, saw some 40,000 nobles cast their votes - a 'nobles' democracy' without parallel in Europe. But the Golden Liberty hardened into paralysis: royal authority was bound ever tighter, the 17th century's wars devastated the state, and the great neighbors - Russia, Prussia, and Austria - learned to exploit its divisions. Under the last king, Stanislaw II August (1764-1795), the Commonwealth declined into a plaything of its neighbors.
para4: The end came in three partitions: 1772, 1793, and 1795. In between, the Commonwealth attempted one of history's most remarkable last stands: the Constitution of 3 May 1791 - the first modern codified constitution in Europe, and the second in the world after the American - came too late to save it. Russia, Prussia, and Austria divided the country among themselves, and Poland-Lithuania vanished from the map for 123 years.

title: The Portuguese Empire
titleline: The Portuguese Empire - The History Web
para1: The Portuguese Empire. Portugal was the first of Europe's global empires - and the last to let go. It began in 1415, when King John I seized Ceuta in North Africa, opening the age of exploration: Portuguese sailors pushed down the African coast with new ships like the caravel, Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope in 1488, and in 1498 Vasco da Gama reached India by sea - the prize of a generation of exploration. In 1500 Pedro Alvares Cabral reached Brazil, and by 1571 a string of naval outposts connected Lisbon all the way to Nagasaki; the colonial trade came to provide about a fifth of Portugal's per-capita income.
para2: The small kingdom could not hold its vast network forever. In 1580 Portugal fell under the Spanish crown in the Iberian Union, and Dutch and English rivals carved away its Asian trade. The Restoration War (1640-1668) recovered independence, and the empire's center of gravity shifted decisively to Brazil, whose gold financed the splendor of the 18th-century court.
para3: The 19th century split the empire: in 1822 Brazil declared its independence, taking with it the empire's richest possession. Portugal refocused on Africa, pushing inland from Angola and Mozambique until the two coasts should meet - the dream of the Rose-Colored Map - until Britain's Ultimatum of 1890 forced its columns to withdraw, a humiliation that nearly brought down the monarchy. In the Scramble's settlement Portugal kept its African colonies, and campaigns of conquest and 'pacification' against resisting peoples continued into the new century.
para4: The 20th century brought revolution at home and war in Africa: the republic proclaimed in 1910 attacked the church and the old monarchical order, and Portugal's entry into the First World War sent its soldiers to fight the Germans in Angola and Mozambique. By 1924 Europe's poorest power still held one of its largest empires - Angola, Mozambique, Guinea, and the old fragments in India, China and the Pacific - the empire of 1415 outlasting the kingdom that had founded it.

title: The Principality of Serbia
titleline: The Principality of Serbia - The History Web
para1: The Principality of Serbia. Modern Serbia rose from the Serbian Revolution against Ottoman rule: Karadjordje's First Serbian Uprising of 1804 failed, but Milos Obrenovic's Second Serbian Uprising of 1815 won what war alone could not - an autonomous Serbian state, recognized by the Ottoman sultan's Hatt-i Sharif of 1830, with Milos as hereditary prince. The new principality, at first covering only the territory of the former Pashaluk of Belgrade, was still nominally Ottoman: it paid a yearly tribute of 2.3 million groschen - about a tenth of the state budget - and Ottoman garrisons remained on its soil.
para2: The principality grew: in 1831-1833 it expanded east, south, and west; a constitution made it a constitutional monarchy from 1838; and from 1866 Serbia began building the first Balkan alliance against the Ottomans. On 18 April 1867 the last Ottoman garrison withdrew from the Belgrade fortress - Serbia's de facto independence - and a new constitution in 1869 defined it as an independent state.
para3: Full international recognition came at the Treaty of Berlin in 1878, which also expanded Serbia to the southeast. In 1882 the principality was raised to the Kingdom of Serbia, with Milan Obrenovic IV as its first king - Serbia's first crown since the medieval empire of Dusan the Mighty.
para4: The principality's story is the pattern of Balkan liberation: revolt, autonomy, independence, kingdom - won over seventy years against Ottoman suzerainty. Its capital had moved from Kragujevac to Belgrade in 1841; even the Ottoman flag that had flown over the Belgrade fortress alongside the Serbian one was finally lowered. Within a generation, the small principality that began as a tribute-paying Ottoman province had become a recognized European kingdom.

title: The Tsardom & Empire of Russia
titleline: The Tsardom & Empire of Russia - The History Web
para1: The Tsardom and Empire of Russia. The Russian Empire grew out of the tsardom that Ivan III had built from the Grand Duchy of Moscow - a centralized state independent of the Great Horde - and that his grandson Ivan IV elevated when he was crowned the first Russian tsar in 1547. The expansion was relentless: between 1550 and 1700, the Russian state grew by an average of 35,000 square kilometers a year, swallowing Siberia - drawn first by its furs - and reaching the Pacific. Under Ivan IV the conquest of the khanates of Kazan and Astrakhan began the transformation of an almost mono-ethnic realm into a multi-ethnic empire; after the Time of Troubles, the Romanov dynasty took the throne.
para2: Peter the Great transformed the tsardom into the Russian Empire, proclaimed in 1721: he fought the wars that made Russia a major European power, moved the capital from Moscow to his new model city of Saint Petersburg, and forced a cultural revolution toward a modern, scientific, Western-oriented state. Catherine the Great (1762-1796) continued his modernization and expanded the empire by conquest, colonization, and diplomacy - including the partitions of Poland.
para3: The 19th century made Russia the gendarme of Europe and exposed its weaknesses: Alexander I helped defeat Napoleon and formed the Holy Alliance, but defeat in the Crimean War (1853-1856) forced reform - above all Alexander II's emancipation of 23 million serfs in 1861. At its height the empire covered about 22.8 million square kilometers - roughly a sixth of the world's land, the third-largest empire in history - stretching from the Baltic to Alaska (colonized 1799-1867), with 126 million people by the 1897 census. Its literature, music, and science flourished even as its politics froze.
para4: The end came fast: the Revolution of 1905 forced the October Manifesto and a semi-constitutional monarchy, but the strains of the First World War brought the empire down in 1917 under Nicholas II, the last tsar. The Revolution of 1905 forced Nicholas II to grant a national parliament, the State Duma, but ultimate power stayed with the tsar. Three centuries of Romanov rule ended in the revolutions of 1917, which toppled the dynasty and plunged the empire into civil war - leaving to its heirs the vast, multi-national inheritance the tsars had built.

title: The Unification of Italy (Risorgimento)
titleline: The Unification of Italy (Risorgimento) - The History Web
para1: The Unification of Italy (Risorgimento). For centuries after the Renaissance, Italy was 'a geographical expression': a patchwork of kingdoms, duchies, and papal states; after 1815 the Austrian Empire directly controlled the Kingdom of Lombardy-Venetia and indirectly the duchies of Parma, Modena, and Tuscany. The Congress of Vienna (1815) confirmed the division, but rebellions in the 1820s and 1830s and the Revolutions of 1848 kept the dream of a united Italy alive - the movement Italians called the Risorgimento, the 'Resurgence.'
para2: National feeling had its literary prophets too: Alessandro Manzoni's novel I Promessi Sposi (1827), a thinly veiled allegory of Austrian rule, even helped fix the Tuscan dialect as the national language. But the unification itself was the work of four very different men: Giuseppe Mazzini, the republican prophet whose writings inspired a generation; Camillo Benso, Count of Cavour, the brilliant prime minister of the Kingdom of Sardinia (Piedmont), who built the alliances and won the wars of diplomacy; Giuseppe Garibaldi, the red-shirted general whose volunteers conquered the Italian south; and King Victor Emmanuel II, the Piedmontese king who became the symbol and sovereign of the new Italy - 'Father of the Fatherland.'
para3: In 1861, after Cavour's wars with Austria and Garibaldi's conquest of the south, the Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed - 17 March is still its anniversary. Venetia and Rome followed, and in 1871 Rome became the capital. But many Italian-speakers in Trentino and Venezia Giulia remained under Austria - the 'unredeemed lands' of Italian irredentism, annexed only in 1918 after the First World War.
para4: The Risorgimento made Italy a nation-state and a great power, but the tensions it papered over - north and south, church and state, monarchy and republic - shaped Italian politics for a century. It remains the founding story of modern Italy: the moment a civilization older than Rome became a country.

title: The Thirty Years' War
titleline: The Thirty Years' War - The History Web
para1: The Thirty Years' War (1618-1648) began in Bohemia, where the Protestant estates feared the Catholic Habsburg succession would revoke their religious liberties, guaranteed by the Letter of Majesty of 1609. In May 1618 Bohemian nobles threw two imperial governors from a window of Prague Castle, the Defenestration of Prague, and set up a rebel state, crowning the Calvinist Frederick V of the Palatinate 'the Winter King'. The Catholic League and Spain crushed the revolt at the White Mountain (1620), and the Palatinate itself was conquered, turning a Bohemian rebellion into a European war as Denmark, then Sweden, then France intervened against the Habsburgs.
para2: Under Emperor Ferdinand II the Catholic powers nearly won outright. Wallenstein's imperial armies and Tilly's Leaguers defeated the Danes at Lutter (1626) and drove them from the war (Peace of Lubeck, 1629), and the Edict of Restitution (1629) ordered Protestant lands confiscated since 1552 returned to the church. The overreach provoked Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden, financed by France, to intervene: his reformed army smashed Tilly at Breitenfeld (1631), swept through Germany, and fell at Lutzen (1632) even in victory. After Wallenstein's assassination in 1634, imperial arms recovered at Nordlingen, but in 1635 Catholic France declared war on Spain openly, and the conflict became a general struggle for the mastery of Europe.
para3: The last thirteen years were the most devastating. Armies of all sides, paid late or never, lived off the land, plundering, burning and spreading famine and plague across Germany. Swedish victory at Wittstock (1636), French victory at Rocroi over the Spanish infantry (1643), and the devastation of regions like the Palatinate and Magdeburg, sacked in 1631 with the loss of most of its people, made the war a byword for horror. Germany lost perhaps a quarter to a third of its population, some regions far more, and the economy of the Holy Roman Empire was set back generations.
para4: Exhaustion brought the Peace of Westphalia (1648), negotiated at Munster and Osnabruck. The settlement confirmed the near-sovereignty of the Empire's princes, including their right to foreign alliances, recognized Calvinism alongside Catholicism and Lutheranism, and awarded Sweden western Pomerania and France lands in Alsace; Switzerland and the Dutch Republic were recognized as independent. Westphalia is conventionally taken to found the European order of sovereign states: it ended the ideal of a unified Christian empire, made France the leading continental power, weakened Habsburg Spain decisively, and established that religious uniformity would no longer decide international politics.

title: The English Civil War and the Protectorate
titleline: The English Civil War and the Protectorate - The History Web
para1: The English Civil War (1642-1651) grew from the breakdown of trust between Charles I and his Parliaments. Charles ruled eleven years without Parliament (1629-1640), raising money by disputed prerogative levies like ship money, while his archbishop, William Laud, imposed ceremonial conformity on the church. When Charles tried to force a new prayer book on Presbyterian Scotland, the Scots rebelled, occupied northern England, and forced him to call Parliament. The Long Parliament (1640) impeached his ministers, abolished prerogative courts, and, after the Irish Catholic revolt of 1641 raised the question of who could be trusted with an army, split between Royalists ('Cavaliers') and Parliamentarians ('Roundheads'). Charles raised his standard at Nottingham in August 1642.
para2: The first war was indecisive until Parliament created the New Model Army (1645), a professional force under Fairfax and Cromwell that destroyed the king's main army at Naseby (1645). Charles surrendered to the Scots, who handed him to Parliament. His secret dealings, and a Scottish invasion on his behalf, provoked the Second Civil War (1648); Cromwell crushed it at Preston, and the army purged Parliament and tried the king. Charles I was executed on 30 January 1649 outside Whitehall, an event that shocked Europe. England was declared a republic, the Commonwealth, while Cromwell's army conquered Ireland, the storming of Drogheda and Wexford with their massacres, and crushed the Scots at Dunbar (1650) and Worcester (1651), where the future Charles II barely escaped.
para3: The Commonwealth's experiments ended in military rule. Cromwell expelled the Rump Parliament in 1653, and after the failure of the Nominated Assembly he accepted the Instrument of Government, becoming Lord Protector. The Protectorate (1653-1658) governed through written constitution, major-generals and a tolerant Protestant church settlement, while Cromwell fought a successful war against Spain, taking Jamaica, and made England a respected power again. Yet the regime rested on the army and on Cromwell's person; Parliament and Protector repeatedly clashed, and republicans, Levellers and Fifth Monarchists all denounced him as a usurper.
para4: Cromwell died in September 1658. His son Richard lasted months before the army deposed him, and in the chaos General George Monck marched from Scotland, restored the surviving members of the Long Parliament, and arranged free elections. In May 1660 Charles II was invited home and the monarchy restored, but the republican decade could not be undone: no English king ever again ruled without Parliament, the New Model's professionalism endured, and the memory of 1649 shaped the constitutional settlement of 1688-1689 and the later British state.

title: The Glorious Revolution
titleline: The Glorious Revolution - The History Web
para1: The Glorious Revolution (1688-1689) replaced the Catholic James II of England with his Protestant daughter Mary and her husband William III of Orange, and settled the English constitution on parliamentary terms. James, succeeding his brother Charles II in 1685, alienated the political nation within three years: he suspended the Test Acts by royal prerogative, kept a standing army near London, promoted Catholics to office, and prosecuted seven bishops who petitioned against his religious policy. The birth of a son, and Catholic heir, in June 1688 ended hopes that his rule was a temporary Catholic interlude, and seven leading Englishmen invited William, stadtholder of the Dutch Republic, to intervene.
para2: William landed at Torbay on 5 November 1688 with a Dutch army of some 15,000, claiming to defend England's religion and liberties and to call a free Parliament. James's army, larger but unreliable, melted as officers and even his daughter Anne deserted; James attempted flight, was allowed to escape to France, and the revolution was effected with almost no fighting in England, though it took real wars to impose in Scotland and Ireland, where the Jacobites were defeated at the Boyne (1690) and Aughrim (1691).
para3: In January 1689 the Convention Parliament declared that James, by fleeing, had abdicated, and offered the crown jointly to William and Mary. The offer came with conditions: the Declaration of Right, enacted as the Bill of Rights (1689), condemned James's abuses and laid down that no monarch could suspend laws, tax without Parliament, maintain a standing army in peacetime without consent, or interfere with elections and parliamentary speech; and it barred Catholics, or anyone married to a Catholic, from the throne. The Toleration Act (1689) gave limited freedom to Protestant dissenters, and the Mutiny Act and annual supply made Parliament a permanent part of government.
para4: The revolution's consequences reached far. In Britain it established parliamentary monarchy, party politics, and the financial revolution, the Bank of England (1694) and a funded national debt, that underwrote Britain's wars and empire. Internationally it brought England into William's Grand Alliance against Louis XIV, beginning the 'Second Hundred Years' War' between Britain and France. In political thought, John Locke's Two Treatises justified government by consent and resistance to tyranny, feeding later liberalism, while Jacobitism, the claim of James's line, kept rebellion alive in Scotland until Culloden (1746). 'Glorious' meant, above all, bloodless and lawful: a revolution made to look like no revolution at all.

title: The War of the Spanish Succession
titleline: The War of the Spanish Succession - The History Web
para1: The War of the Spanish Succession (1701-1714) decided who would inherit the vast empire of the last Spanish Habsburg, Charles II: Spain itself, the Spanish Netherlands, most of Italy, and colonies from the Caribbean to the Pacific. Charles died childless in 1700, leaving his crown by will to Philip of Anjou, grandson of Louis XIV of France. The Austrian Habsburgs claimed it for the Archduke Charles. Louis's acceptance for his grandson, and his provocations, recognizing the Stuart pretender, seizing the Spanish Netherlands' barrier fortresses, and monopolizing American trade, drove Britain, the Dutch Republic and Austria into the Grand Alliance, fearing a Bourbon super-state.
para2: The war was fought on five fronts. In the Low Countries and Germany, the Duke of Marlborough won a string of victories unmatched in British military history: Blenheim (1704), which saved Vienna and destroyed the Franco-Bavarian army; Ramillies (1706), which conquered the Spanish Netherlands in a day; Oudenarde (1708); and the Pyrrhic Malplaquet (1709). In Spain the Allies landed the Archduke Charles as 'Charles III', twice took Madrid but could not hold it, and were broken at Almansa (1707) and Brihuega-Villaviciosa (1710), leaving Philip V master of the Spanish heartland. At sea, Britain took Gibraltar (1704) and Minorca (1708), and in the north the war merged with the Great Northern War's diplomacy.
para3: Exhaustion, famine in France's terrible winter of 1709, and political change ended the war. In Britain the Tories, hostile to continental war, won power in 1710 and dismissed Marlborough; and when the Archduke Charles unexpectedly became Emperor Charles VI in 1711, British opinion refused to trade a Bourbon Spain for a Habsburg one. Britain negotiated separately, and the Treaties of Utrecht (1713) and Rastatt and Baden (1714) settled the peace: Philip V kept Spain and the Indies, renouncing the French succession for himself and his line; Austria took the Spanish Netherlands and most of Spanish Italy, with Sicily going to Savoy; Britain kept Gibraltar and Minorca and won the asiento, the contract to supply enslaved Africans to Spanish America.
para4: Utrecht redrew Europe. The Spanish Empire was partitioned, the balance of power became the explicit principle of European diplomacy, and Britain emerged as the great naval and commercial winner. France was humbled but not broken, Austria gained a new Italian empire it could barely defend, and the Dutch barrier against France was entrenched. Spain, meanwhile, remained under the Bourbon dynasty Philip founded, which reformed the state along French lines and rules Spain to the present day, with interruptions.

title: The Seven Years' War
titleline: The Seven Years' War - The History Web
para1: The Seven Years' War (1756-1763) was the first truly global war, fought in Europe, North America, India, the Caribbean and the Pacific. Its immediate cause in Europe was the 'diplomatic revolution' of 1756: centuries of Franco-Habsburg rivalry ended in an alliance between Austria and France, joined by Russia, to crush Prussia, whose king Frederick II had seized Silesia from Maria Theresa of Austria in 1740. Britain aligned with Prussia, subsidizing Frederick while fighting France for empire overseas. Frederick struck first, invading Saxony in 1756 to forestall the coalition against him.
para2: Frederick's Prussia survived by generalship against encircling enemies four times its size. In 1757 he destroyed a French and imperial army at Rossbach in under an hour and a month later routed the Austrians at Leuthen; but the Russians won at Gross-Jagersdorf and Kunersdorf (1759), where the Prussian army was annihilated and Frederick contemplated suicide, and Austrian and Russian armies briefly occupied Berlin (1760). The 'miracle of the House of Brandenburg' came in 1762 when the pro-Prussian Peter III succeeded Elizabeth in Russia, made peace, and even returned conquests; Sweden then dropped out, and Austria, bankrupted, made peace at Hubertusburg (1763), restoring the status quo: Prussia kept Silesia and emerged confirmed as a great power.
para3: In North America, where the war had effectively begun in 1754 with skirmishes in the Ohio valley, France initially prevailed, but British money, sea power and colonial manpower turned the tide: Louisbourg fell in 1758, and in 1759 Wolfe defeated Montcalm on the Plains of Abraham outside Quebec, both generals dying, and Montreal surrendered in 1760, ending New France. In India, Robert Clive's victory at Plassey (1757) made the East India Company master of Bengal, and Pondicherry fell in 1761. Spain, entering late on France's side, lost Havana and Manila to British expeditions in 1762.
para4: The Peace of Paris (1763) redrew the world map: France ceded Canada and all territory east of the Mississippi to Britain and Louisiana to Spain, and left India reduced to a few trading posts; Spain ceded Florida and received Louisiana and Havana back. Britain became the dominant colonial and naval power, and the costs of victory, taxing the American colonies to pay the war's debt, set in train the crisis that produced the American Revolution a decade later. In Europe the war confirmed Prussia's survival and Russia's arrival as a decisive player, and it left Austria and France nursing debts and grievances that would surface again in the revolutionary era.
source2label: World History Encyclopedia: Seven Years' War

title: The Congress of Vienna and the Restoration
titleline: The Congress of Vienna and the Restoration - The History Web
para1: The Congress of Vienna (September 1814 - June 1815) was the great peace conference that rebuilt Europe after more than twenty years of Revolutionary and Napoleonic war. Nearly every state and court of Europe sent representatives to the Austrian capital, where the Austrian foreign minister Metternich, Britain's Castlereagh, Prussia's Hardenberg, Russia's Tsar Alexander I, and, most skillfully, France's Talleyrand, representing the defeated power, bargained over the map while the city danced. The guiding principles were legitimacy, restoring the old dynasties Napoleon had displaced, the balance of power, so no state could again dominate Europe, and compensation for the victors' losses and efforts.
para2: The territorial settlement redrew the continent. France returned roughly to its 1792 borders. To contain it, the Dutch Republic and the Austrian Netherlands were merged into a Kingdom of the Netherlands, Prussia received the Rhineland, and Austria kept Lombardy and Venetia. Austria and Prussia were compensated in Italy and Germany for the Polish lands lost to Russia, which kept most of Napoleon's Grand Duchy of Warsaw as 'Congress Poland'. The Holy Roman Empire, dissolved in 1806, was not restored; instead thirty-nine German states formed a loose German Confederation under Austrian presidency. Sweden kept Norway, taken from Denmark, and Britain kept Malta, the Cape of Good Hope and Ceylon.
para3: The negotiations were interrupted in March 1815 by Napoleon's escape from Elba and his Hundred Days, which ended at Waterloo in June; the second Treaty of Paris (1815) then imposed harsher terms on France, an indemnity and an army of occupation. To preserve the settlement, Alexander I promoted the Holy Alliance of Christian monarchs, while Austria, Prussia, Russia and Britain formed the Quadruple Alliance, pledging to meet in congresses to maintain the peace, the beginning of the 'Congress System' at Aix-la-Chapelle, Troppau and Laibach.
para4: The Vienna settlement gave Europe nearly forty years without a general war, an achievement no previous peace had matched. Its conservative order, defended by Metternich's Carlsbad Decrees and occasional interventions, suppressed the liberal and national movements the revolutionary era had unleashed, but only until they burst out in 1830 and 1848. Belgium seceded from the Netherlands in 1830, and German and Italian unification later demolished the map, yet the balance-of-power system Vienna created, and the idea of settling affairs by congress diplomacy, shaped European statecraft to 1914 and beyond.

title: The Revolutions of 1848
titleline: The Revolutions of 1848 - The History Web
para1: The Revolutions of 1848 were a wave of uprisings that swept across Europe, the most widespread revolutionary year in its history. Behind them lay economic crisis, the potato blight and harvest failures of 1845-1847, industrial slump and unemployment, combined with demands for constitutions, national independence and, in the west, wider suffrage. The spark came in France: in February 1848 the 'banquet campaign' against Louis-Philippe's corruption brought down the July Monarchy in three days of Paris barricades, and the Second Republic was proclaimed, with national workshops for the unemployed and universal male suffrage.
para2: The fire spread within weeks. In Vienna, students and workers drove Metternich himself into exile (March 1848); Hungary under Kossuth won a constitution from the frightened emperor; Czechs, Croats, Romanians and Italians of the empire asserted their own national claims. In Berlin, Frederick William IV of Prussia, after street fighting, promised a constitution, and a German National Assembly gathered in Frankfurt to write one for a united Germany. In Italy, Milan expelled the Austrians in the Five Days, Venice declared a republic, and Piedmont-Sardinia went to war for Italian independence, while the pope fled Rome, where Mazzini's Roman Republic was proclaimed in 1849.
para3: The revolutions then divided and were crushed one by one. In France, the June Days (1848) saw the army and provincial militias massacre the Parisian workers after the workshops were closed, and in December Louis-Napoleon Bonaparte was elected president, ending as emperor in 1852. In the Habsburg lands, the army retook Vienna (October 1848) and Prague, the new emperor Franz Joseph abolished the March constitution, and Hungary's full declaration of independence was destroyed in 1849 by Austrian and Russian armies, Russia intervening to save the monarchy. The Frankfurt Parliament, after a year of debate, offered the German crown to Frederick William IV, who refused to 'pick up a crown from the gutter'; the assembly dissolved, and Prussian troops finished off the last risings. In Italy, Austria defeated Piedmont at Custoza (1848) and Novara (1849), and France restored the pope by taking Rome.
para4: The revolutions failed almost everywhere in their immediate aims, but 1848 changed Europe permanently. Serfdom was abolished for good in the Austrian Empire; universal male suffrage, though abused, had come to France; constitutions survived in Prussia and Piedmont; and the movements for German and Italian unity learned to look not to assemblies but to 'blood and iron' and Cavour's diplomacy, achieving within a generation by war and statecraft what the revolutionaries of 1848 could not. Marx and Engels, whose Communist Manifesto appeared as the revolutions began, drew the lesson that would feed the socialist movements of the next century.

title: The Crimean War
titleline: The Crimean War - The History Web
para1: The Crimean War (1853-1856) pitted Russia against the Ottoman Empire, France, Britain and eventually Sardinia-Piedmont, the only great-power war in Europe between 1815 and 1914. Its immediate quarrel was almost farcical, rival rights of Catholic and Orthodox monks over the Holy Places in Jerusalem, but the substance was the 'Eastern Question': Tsar Nicholas I claimed a protectorate over the Ottoman Empire's Orthodox Christians and expected its collapse, while France championed the Catholics and Britain was determined to block Russian expansion toward the Mediterranean. When the Ottomans refused his demands, Nicholas occupied the Danubian Principalities (Moldavia and Wallachia) in 1853, and the Ottoman Empire declared war after Russia destroyed its fleet at Sinope (November 1853).
para2: France and Britain entered in March 1854, and after Austria's pressure forced Russia to evacuate the principalities, the allies decided to strike at Russia's naval power itself: they landed in Crimea in September 1854 to take Sevastopol, home of the Black Sea Fleet. The war's battles became legends of mismanagement and endurance: the Alma (September 1854), a bloody allied victory; Balaclava (October 1854), with the thin red line of Highlanders and the disastrous Charge of the Light Brigade, a cavalry attack misdirected into a valley of guns; and Inkerman (November 1854), the 'soldiers' battle' in the fog, after which the allies, unprepared for winter, nearly died of cold, hunger and disease in their camps.
para3: The siege of Sevastopol lasted nearly a year, its earthworks and artillery foreshadowing industrial siege warfare. The public storm over conditions, exposed by the first great war correspondents like William Howard Russell of The Times, brought down the Aberdeen government in Britain, and Florence Nightingale's nursing mission at Scutari cut the horrific death rate from disease and founded modern nursing. Sardinia joined the allies in 1855 to win a seat at the peace table for the Italian cause. After the fall of the Malakoff redoubt (September 1855) the Russians blew up Sevastopol's remaining forts and evacuated; the accession of Alexander II, after Nicholas I died in March 1855, opened the way to peace.
para4: By the Treaty of Paris (1856) the Black Sea was neutralized, forbidding Russian warships and bases, a humiliation Russia nursed until it repudiated the clause in 1870, and the Ottoman Empire was admitted to the European concert with guarantees of its integrity. The war's costs, some 750,000 dead, mostly of disease, and shattered finances, drove Russia's great reforms, above all the emancipation of the serfs (1861). It ended the post-1815 conservative solidarity of Russia and Austria, leaving Austria isolated when the wars of Italian and German unification came, and it announced modern war: railways, telegraphs, rifled muskets, trench lines and war photography had all arrived.

title: The Swedish Empire
titleline: The Swedish Empire - The History Web
para1: The Swedish Empire, the stormaktstiden or 'age of great power', made Sweden the dominant power of the Baltic in the seventeenth century. Its foundations were laid under Gustavus Vasa, who broke the Kalmar Union in 1523, seized church wealth in the Reformation, and built a centralized monarchy, and by the conquests of his grandsons in the eastern Baltic. The empire proper began with Gustavus Adolphus (1611-1632): reformed army, national conscription, mobile artillery, and battlefield drill made Sweden's army the most modern in Europe. His intervention in the Thirty Years' War, from the victory of Breitenfeld (1631) to his death at Lutzen (1632), made Sweden the arbiter of Germany.
para2: The Peace of Westphalia (1648) rewarded Sweden with western Pomerania, Bremen-Verden and Wismar, giving it control of the mouths of the Oder, Elbe and Weser. Under Charles X Gustav, Sweden seized Scania, Halland and Blekinge from Denmark (Treaty of Roskilde, 1658), closing the Danish strait empire, and under Charles XI the realm was consolidated: the reduction of 1680 expropriated the great nobles' crown lands, financing a standing army and the allotment system, indelningsverket, that quartered soldiers on farms. The Baltic had become a Swedish lake, and the empire stretched from Norway to Estonia and Ingria.
para3: Charles XI's son Charles XII inherited the empire in 1697 at fifteen, and the neighbors he had humbled, Denmark, Saxony-Poland and Peter the Great's Russia, attacked in 1700 to recover their losses. The young king's response was astonishing: he knocked Denmark out at once, annihilated a far larger Russian army at Narva (1700), then spent six years conquering Poland and Saxony, deposing Augustus the Strong. But in 1709, deep in Ukraine, his army was destroyed at Poltava, and the empire collapsed around him: Russia occupied the Baltic provinces, Hanover and Prussia took the German lands, and Charles, returning from Turkish exile, was killed besieging Fredriksten in 1718. The treaties of Stockholm and Nystad (1720-1721) stripped Sweden of everything except Finland and part of Pomerania.
para4: The empire's fall made Sweden a minor power and Russia the new master of the Baltic. At home, the death of Charles XII ended royal absolutism and opened the Age of Liberty (1719-1772), a remarkable experiment in parliamentary party government under the Hats and Caps, ended by Gustav III's coup. Sweden lost Finland to Russia in 1809, gained Norway in compensation in 1814, and, under Bernadotte, adopted the neutrality it has largely kept since. The stormaktstiden remained Sweden's national myth: proof that a poor country of barely a million people could, by military organization and state discipline, briefly rule an empire.

title: The Cossack Hetmanate
titleline: The Cossack Hetmanate - The History Web
para1: The Cossack Hetmanate was the semi-autonomous Cossack state that ruled central Ukraine for over a century after the uprising of Bohdan Khmelnytsky in 1648. Its roots lay in the Zaporozhian Cossacks, the self-governing warrior host 'beyond the rapids' of the Dnieper, runaway serfs, frontiersmen and freebooters who raided the Crimean Khanate and the Ottoman Black Sea, and who chafed under Polish-Lithuanian rule that treated them as a resource to be registered and limited. Tensions over noble encroachment, the curbing of the Cossack register, and the persecution of the Orthodox faith in the Commonwealth's borderlands exploded in 1648, when Khmelnytsky, wronged by a Polish official, allied with the Crimean Tatars and destroyed two Polish armies at Zhovti Vody and Korsun.
para2: The revolt became a war of liberation that redrew eastern Europe. Khmelnytsky's armies, swollen by peasants, swept the Commonwealth's eastern lands in upheavals that included massacres of Polish nobles and of Jews, tens of thousands of whom died as agents of the hated regime. Unable to win the war outright against a resurgent Poland, Khmelnytsky sought a protector, and by the Treaty of Pereyaslav (1654) he placed the Cossack Host under the tsar of Muscovy, an act whose meaning, alliance or submission, Russia and Ukraine have argued ever since. The Russo-Polish War that followed (1654-1667) devastated Ukraine, and the Truce of Andrusovo divided it: the left bank of the Dnieper and Kiev to Russia, the right bank to Poland.
para3: In the left-bank territories the Hetmanate survived as an autonomous state under its elected hetmans, with its own regiments, chancellery, courts and foreign relations, within the tsar's growing empire. Its golden age came under Ivan Mazepa (1687-1709): Cossack baroque churches and schools flourished, the Kyiv-Mohyla Academy made Kiev an intellectual center, and the hetman governed as a prince. But Peter the Great's demands in the Great Northern War, Cossack lives spent in northern campaigns, tsarist interference in elections, pushed Mazepa to defect to Charles XII of Sweden in 1708. Poltava destroyed them both: Mazepa died in exile, and Peter's reprisals razed the Zaporozhian Sich and tightened the screws.
para4: After Mazepa, autonomy was dismantled in stages: Peter imposed a Russian 'Little Russian Collegium', Catherine II abolished the hetmanate entirely in 1764 and the Sich itself in 1775, and serfdom was extended over the formerly free Cossack lands. The Hetmanate's regimental territories became the guberniyas of the Russian Empire. Yet the Hetmanate left a durable legacy: the office, the regiments and the Cossack myth became central to Ukrainian national identity, and the memory of Pereyaslav and Mazepa, partnership or treachery, submission or sovereignty, still frames the way Ukraine and Russia tell their shared history.

title: Enlightened Absolutism
titleline: Enlightened Absolutism - The History Web
para1: The Enlightenment was the eighteenth-century movement of reason that challenged the intellectual foundations of the old European order, and enlightened absolutism was the monarchs' attempt to use its tools without its conclusions. Its origins lay in the scientific revolution of the seventeenth century, Newton's ordered universe, and in the empiricism of Locke: if nature ran by discoverable laws and knowledge came from experience, then society, government, religion and law could be questioned and improved by reason rather than inherited by tradition. France was its heartland: Voltaire's campaigns against religious fanaticism and legal torture, Montesquieu's analysis of the separation of powers (1748), and the great Encyclopedie of Diderot and d'Alembert (1751-1772) spread critical thought through the reading public of salons, coffeehouses and clandestine print.
para2: The philosophes attacked privilege, superstition and censorship, though few were democrats or atheists. Rousseau went furthest, arguing in The Social Contract (1762) that legitimate government rested on the general will, and his celebration of natural virtue made him the prophet of both romanticism and revolution. Beyond France, the movement took national colors: Hume and Adam Smith in Scotland, whose Wealth of Nations (1776) founded economics; Beccaria's On Crimes and Punishments (1764), which reformed European penal law; Kant in Prussia defining enlightenment as the courage to think for oneself. Everywhere the new public sphere of journals, academies, masonic lodges and lending libraries created opinion as a political force.
para3: The absolute monarchs of Europe could not ignore the new ideas, and several adopted them, on their own terms. Frederick II of Prussia, flute-playing correspondent of Voltaire, abolished torture, decreed religious toleration, codified Prussian law and called himself the first servant of the state, while strengthening the army and the Junker monarchy. Catherine II of Russia corresponded with Diderot, drew on Montesquieu and Beccaria for her Nakaz (1767), bought libraries and founded schools, while extending serfdom to its widest reach and crushing Pugachev's revolt. Joseph II of Austria went furthest: thousands of decrees abolishing serfdom, dissolving monasteries, imposing toleration (1781) and Germanizing administration, a 'revolution from above' that provoked such resistance that his brother Leopold II had to undo much of it. Spain under Charles III, Portugal under Pombal, and Tuscany under Leopold also enacted 'enlightened' reforms.
para4: The partnership of reason and power had its limits, and they were soon exposed. Enlightened absolutism accepted the ends of efficiency and toleration but never the means of self-government; when the American colonies applied Locke against the king (1776) and France applied Rousseau against the Bastille (1789), the monarchs abandoned the philosophes and embraced reaction. Yet the Enlightenment had changed the terms of European politics permanently: reason of state now had to speak the language of utility, rights and public opinion, and the age's reforms, legal codes, religious toleration, secular education, the critique of torture, survived the revolutions they helped to cause.
