title: The Papal States in the Age of Revolutions
titleline: The Papal States in the Age of Revolutions - The History Web
para1: The Papal States entered the modern era as one of Europe's oldest political bodies, territories across central Italy ruled by the popes as temporal sovereigns since the eighth century. The wars of the French Revolution shattered their world: French armies occupied Rome twice, carried off Pope Pius VI as a prisoner in 1798, and annexed the Papal States outright in 1809, imprisoning Pius VII after he excommunicated Napoleon. The Congress of Vienna (1815) restored the pope's lands almost intact, and for the next half century the papal government, administered by clerics, guarding against secret societies, railways and modern political ideas alike, became the byword of conservative reaction in Europe.
para2: Italian unification destroyed the temporal power piece by piece. The revolutions of 1848 drove Pius IX from Rome; the Roman Republic of Mazzini and Garibaldi ruled until French troops restored him in 1849. In 1860 the armies of Piedmont-Sardinia annexed the Romagna, the Marches and Umbria, leaving the pope only Rome and its countryside, defended by French bayonets and Catholic volunteers. When France withdrew its garrison during the Franco-Prussian War, Italian troops breached the Porta Pia on 20 September 1870 and took Rome, which became Italy's capital. Pius IX refused the Italian government's Law of Guarantees, declared himself 'prisoner of the Vatican', and forbade Catholics, under the non expedit, from taking part in Italian political life.
para3: The 'Roman Question' festered for decade after decade. Successive popes never set foot outside the Vatican walls, the non expedit kept faithful Italians out of national politics, and every Italian government maintained the unanswered Law of Guarantees. The First World War, fought between Catholic Austria and Italy, sharpened the isolation: Benedict XV's peace note of 1917 was ignored by the belligerents, and the new pope Pius XI, elected in 1922, set about rebuilding the Church's missions - and looking for a way to end the quarrel with Italy.
para4: By 1924 the standoff had lasted fifty-four years: the pope sovereign over a palace and a garden, Italy's capital seated in the city the popes still claimed, and no settlement in sight - though discreet contacts had begun. The Roman Question had shaped two generations of Catholic politics, from the culture wars of Bismarck's Germany to the anticlerical laws of republican France, and it remained, as it had been since 1870, the open wound of the Italian state.

title: The Balkan Wars
titleline: The Balkan Wars - The History Web
para1: The Balkan Wars of 1912-1913 destroyed Ottoman power in Europe and set the stage for the First World War. Behind them lay the slow Ottoman retreat from the Balkans and the ambitions of the new Christian states, Serbia, Bulgaria, Greece and Montenegro, whose peoples still lived under Ottoman rule in Macedonia, Albania and Thrace. In 1912, encouraged by Russian diplomacy and by Italy's war with the Ottomans in Libya, the four states formed the Balkan League, and in October 1912 they attacked together. The First Balkan War was a rout: the Serbs took Kosovo and Macedonia, the Greeks took Thessaloniki, just ahead of the Bulgarians, and the Bulgarians drove to within miles of Constantinople, while the great powers recognized an independent Albania to keep Serbia off the Adriatic.
para2: The victors immediately fell out over the spoils. Bulgaria, which had done the heaviest fighting, claimed most of Macedonia; Serbia, shut out of Albania, demanded compensation there; Greece and Romania also held claims against Sofia. When negotiations failed, Bulgaria attacked its former allies on 29 June 1913, opening the Second Balkan War. Serbia, Greece, Montenegro and Romania, which seized southern Dobruja, all counterattacked, and the Ottoman Empire returned to recover Adrianople (Edirne). Within a month Bulgaria was crushed and forced to sign the Treaty of Bucharest (August 1913), losing territory on every side.
para3: The wars doubled the size of Serbia, Greece, Montenegro and Romania, cut the Ottoman Empire back to a corner of Thrace, and confirmed Albanian independence. But they left three poisonous legacies. First, a humiliated Bulgaria nursed revenge, joining the Central Powers in 1915 to recover what it had lost. Second, a triumphant Serbia, now twice its size, terrified Austria-Hungary, which saw South Slav nationalism, armed by Belgrade, reaching into its own provinces; the Sarajevo assassination of June 1914 grew directly from the wars' settlement. Third, the wars introduced mass ethnic violence into southeastern Europe: villages burned, populations expelled, atrocities documented by an international commission of 1914 that read like a preview of the century to come.
para4: The Balkan Wars also revealed the great powers' near-paralysis: Austria-Hungary mobilized, Russia backed Serbia, and the Concert of Europe, through the London Conference of ambassadors, managed only to draw Albania's borders while the fighting decided everything else. When the next Balkan crisis came in July 1914, no one believed diplomacy would contain it, and the alliance system that had kept the peace for forty years pulled Europe into a general war in a matter of weeks.

title: Russia from Decembrists to 1905
titleline: Russia from Decembrists to 1905 - The History Web
para1: The Revolution of 1905 was Russia's first great revolutionary crisis, the 'dress rehearsal', as Lenin called it, for 1917. Its causes lay in the contradictions of the tsarist autocracy: a rapidly industrializing economy and an oppressed working class living in squalor, land-hungry peasants, restive national minorities on the empire's edges, and an intelligentsia excluded from political life, all ruled by Nicholas II, a weak tsar committed to unlimited autocracy. Defeat in the Russo-Japanese War (1904-1905) exposed the regime's incompetence to the world, and on 22 January 1905 the crisis broke: troops fired on a peaceful procession of St Petersburg workers marching with icons and petitions to the Winter Palace, led by the priest Father Gapon. 'Bloody Sunday' killed hundreds and destroyed the myth of the benevolent tsar.
para2: The empire erupted. Strikes spread from city to city, a general strike in October paralyzed the railways; peasants burned manor houses; mutinies shook the armed forces, most famously on the battleship Potemkin in Odessa in June; soviets, workers' councils, appeared for the first time, the St Petersburg Soviet led briefly by the young Leon Trotsky; and from Poland to the Caucasus the non-Russian peoples rose. Every strand of opposition, liberal zemstvo men demanding a constitution, Socialist Revolutionaries among the peasants, Marxist Social Democrats, national movements, surged at once against the autocracy.
para3: Faced with the general strike and a still-unreliable army, Nicholas II conceded: the October Manifesto (30 October 1905) promised civil liberties and an elected parliament, the State Duma, with legislative powers. The concession split the opposition: liberals accepted and went home, workers and socialists fought on, and in December the Moscow Soviet's armed uprising was crushed by artillery in the streets of Presnya. With the army loyal and the regime's enemies divided, the government regained control through 1906, backed by pogroms against Jews and revolutionaries, field courts-martial and mass arrests, the 'Stolypin necktie' of the gallows.
para4: The Fundamental Laws of April 1906 then hollowed out the promised constitution: the tsar kept control of the army, foreign policy and ministers, and could dismiss the Duma at will. Four Dumas were elected on ever-narrower franchises, and Stolypin's agrarian reforms tried to build a class of loyal peasant proprietors while thousands of revolutionaries went to Siberia or exile. The 1905 revolution failed, but it had shown that the autocracy could be shaken: the soviet was invented, the parties were battle-tested, and the workers and soldiers who made 1905 would make February and October 1917.

title: The Eighty Years' War
titleline: The Eighty Years' War - The History Web
para1: The Eighty Years' War (1568-1648), also called the Dutch Revolt, created the Dutch Republic out of rebellion against the Spanish Habsburgs. The Seventeen Provinces of the Netherlands, among Europe's richest and most urbanized lands, were inherited by Philip II of Spain, whose government attacked the privileges of the provinces' estates, quartered Spanish garrisons, planned new bishoprics, and sent the Inquisition against spreading Protestantism. Resistance hardened after 1566, when the nobles' petition of the Compromise was dismissed, the petitioners proudly adopting the slur 'Beggars', and Calvinist mobs in the 'Iconoclastic Fury' smashed church images across the provinces. Philip answered with the Duke of Alba's Army of Flanders and the Council of Troubles, which executed the counts Egmont and Hornes in Brussels in 1568 and drove thousands into exile.
para2: William of Orange, the Silent, organized the revolt from exile, and in 1572 the Sea Beggars seized Brielle, triggering general insurrection in Holland and Zeeland. Alba's terror, the sack of Mechelen, Zutphen and Naarden, the siege and massacre of Haarlem and the relief of Leiden, whose dikes were cut to drown the siege, failed to break the northern provinces, united behind William in 1576's Pacification of Ghent after the Spanish Fury at Antwerp horrified the whole Netherlands. But Parma's reconquest of the Catholic south in the 1580s, taking Antwerp in 1585 after a brilliant siege, split the provinces permanently: the south remained Spanish, the future Belgium; the seven northern provinces had formed the Union of Utrecht (1579) and in 1581, by the Act of Abjuration, formally deposed Philip, Europe's first modern declaration of independence.
para3: After William's assassination in 1584, the young republic survived through trade wealth, sea power and the military reforms of Maurice of Nassau, who with Oldenbarnevelt built a professional army that retook Breda and the eastern fortresses. England's war with Spain, ending in the Armada's defeat (1588), relieved the pressure, and the Dutch took the war to the sea and the world: the East India Company (1602) and West India Company (1621) seized Portuguese and Spanish possessions from Brazil to Indonesia. A Twelve Years' Truce (1609) acknowledged facts without recognition, but war resumed with the Thirty Years' War, whose Dutch theater saw Frederick Henry's sieges, the Battle of the Downs (1639) destroying Spanish sea power, and the Franco-Dutch alliance against Spain.
para4: The Peace of Munster, part of Westphalia (30 January 1648), ended the war: Spain finally recognized the independence of the Republic of the Seven United Netherlands, keeping the Scheldt closed to strangle Antwerp for Amsterdam's benefit. The war had created Europe's most unusual state: a merchant republic without a king, tolerant by the standards of the age, the financial and naval center of the world, whose Golden Age of Rembrandt, Vermeer and Spinoza was built while the fighting continued. The southern Netherlands stayed under Spanish, then Austrian, rule until 1794.

title: The Great Northern War
titleline: The Great Northern War - The History Web
para1: The Great Northern War (1700-1721) decided whether Sweden or Russia would dominate northeastern Europe. Sweden's Baltic empire, stretching from Bremen to Narva, had humbled its neighbors, and in 1697 the fifteen-year-old Charles XII inherited it. Three of them, Denmark, Augustus the Strong's Saxony-Poland, and Peter the Great's Russia, allied to dismember the empire while the boy-king reigned. Charles answered with a speed that stunned Europe: he landed near Copenhagen and knocked Denmark out of the war in August 1700, then shipped to Estonia and in a November blizzard annihilated a Russian army four times his size at Narva, capturing its guns and its generals. Peter's new model army had been destroyed in an afternoon.
para2: Instead of marching on Moscow, Charles turned west to deal with Augustus, whose Saxon and Polish territories he spent six years conquering. By the Treaty of Altranstadt (1706) he deposed Augustus from the Polish throne and imposed his own candidate, Stanislaus Leszczynski. The delay proved fatal. Peter rebuilt his army on the Swedish model, took Narva and Dorpat, founded St Petersburg on conquered Ingrian soil (1703), and drew Charles into a war of attrition. When Charles finally invaded Russia in 1708, allied with the Cossack hetman Mazepa, Peter denied him supplies, winter and Russian scorched-earth columns bled the march, and at Poltava on 8 July 1709 Peter destroyed the Swedish army outright. Charles fled into Ottoman exile at Bender, where he spent five years trying to draw the sultan into the war.
para3: While Charles was away, the empire he had defended fell apart. Augustus returned to Poland; Denmark re-entered the war; Hanover, Prussia and Russia took the Swedish possessions in Germany and the Baltic; and Peter's new fleet defeated the Swedes at Gangut (1714). Charles returned to a ruined kingdom in 1715, defended Stralsund, and was killed by a shot through the head besieging Fredriksten in Norway in 1718. His sister Ulrika Eleonora and then her husband Frederick I made peace piecemeal: the Treaties of Stockholm (1719-1720) ceded Bremen-Verden to Hanover and part of Pomerania to Prussia, and the Treaty of Nystad (1721) ceded Livonia, Estonia, Ingria and eastern Karelia to Russia.
para4: Nystad ended Sweden's age as a great power and confirmed Russia's arrival as one: Peter proclaimed himself emperor the same year, and St Petersburg became the new capital of a Russia that now dominated the Baltic and, increasingly, the politics of Poland, Germany and Scandinavia. The war also transformed both losers and winners: Sweden turned from absolutism to its parliamentary Age of Liberty, while Russia's victory rested on the forced Westernization, conscription, industry and a fleet built from nothing, that would define the empire for two centuries.

title: The Greek War of Independence
titleline: The Greek War of Independence - The History Web
para1: The Greek War of Independence (1821-1832) freed the first nation of the Ottoman Empire's European provinces and made Greece an independent kingdom. Its background was the national revival of the eighteenth century: the Greeks of the diaspora, of the Phanariot administration and of the merchant fleets, the ideas of the French Revolution, and the secret society Filiki Eteria, founded in Odessa in 1814, which organized the rising. In March 1821 Alexander Ypsilantis crossed into the Danubian Principalities hoping for Russian support, and was crushed; but in the Peloponnese the revolt proclaimed on 25 March spread like fire. By autumn the rebels held most of the peninsula: Tripolitsa fell in October 1821, amid massacres of its Muslim inhabitants that were answered by Ottoman reprisals, above all the execution of the Patriarch Gregory V in Constantinople and the massacres of Chios (1822), where tens of thousands were killed or enslaved.
para2: The revolution nearly destroyed itself through civil war: rival governments, military chiefs and regional factions fought two civil wars in 1823-1825 even as they fought the sultan. Mahmud II called in his powerful vassal Muhammad Ali of Egypt, whose son Ibrahim Pasha landed with a modern army in 1825 and reconquered the Peloponnese systematically; Missolonghi, defended for a year, fell in April 1826, its garrison dying in a famous sortie that Byron's death there in 1824 had already made a European symbol. Athens fell in 1827, and the revolution survived only in a few pockets. Greece was saved by the powers: Britain, France and Russia, their publics ablaze with philhellenism, their cabinets pursuing advantage, mediated, and when negotiations failed their combined fleet destroyed the Ottoman-Egyptian fleet at Navarino (October 1827), the last great battle of the age of sail.
para3: Russia's declaration of war (1828) and its victories on the Danube forced the sultan to terms. The Treaty of Adrianople (1829) gave Greece autonomy, and the London Protocol (1830), following the assassination of the first governor, the capable Ioannis Kapodistrias, made Greece an independent kingdom under the powers' guarantee. In 1832 the seventeen-year-old Bavarian prince Otto arrived as king with a Bavarian administration; his autocratic rule provoked a constitution in 1843, and the kingdom's borders, which excluded most Greeks, in Thessaly, Epirus, Macedonia, Crete and the islands, drove a century of irredentism under the 'Megali Idea'.
para4: The Greek revolution's significance reached far beyond the Aegean. It was the first successful national revolution in Ottoman Europe, the model and the precedent for the Serbs, Romanians and Bulgarians who followed; it demonstrated that the Concert of Europe would not always defend the territorial status quo against national revolt; and the philhellenic movement, volunteers, loans, poems, made nationalism a European cause. Modern Greece, though small and repeatedly rescued, had shown that the empires of the old order could be broken.

title: The Russo-Turkish Wars
titleline: The Russo-Turkish Wars - The History Web
para1: The Russo-Turkish Wars were the long series of conflicts, twelve major wars between 1568 and 1917, through which Russia expanded southward at the Ottoman Empire's expense. The early clashes were frontier wars over the steppe: Astrakhan, the Azov fortress, and the Crimean Khanate, the Ottomans' vassal, whose slave-raiding horsemen burned Moscow itself in 1571. Peter the Great took Azov (1696), lost it again on the Pruth (1711), and the eighteenth century turned the wars into a systematic Russian advance: by the Treaty of Kucuk Kaynarca (1774), after Catherine the Great's armies won at Kagul, Russia gained a foothold on the Black Sea, the right to navigate it, and a claimed protectorate over Ottoman Orthodox Christians. Nine years later Catherine annexed Crimea outright.
para2: The nineteenth century made the wars the core of the 'Eastern Question'. Russia presented itself as the protector of the sultan's Orthodox subjects, Greeks, Serbs, Romanians, Bulgarians, while Britain and France feared the Straits falling into Russian hands and repeatedly propped the Ottoman Empire up. The wars of 1806-1812 and 1828-1829 gave Russia Bessarabia and the Danube's mouth and helped free Greece; the war of 1853-1856, the Crimean War, was Russia's great reversal, when Britain, France and Sardinia intervened to save the sultan and neutralized the Black Sea. Russia answered with expansion in the Caucasus and Central Asia, and with pan-Slav support for the Balkan Christians.
para3: The great war came in 1877. After the Ottomans crushed Bulgarian and Serbian risings with massacres that outraged Europe, Alexander II declared war. Russian armies crossed the Danube, were held for months at Plevna by Osman Pasha's heroic defense, then broke through the Balkan mountains in winter to within reach of Constantinople. The Treaty of San Stefano (March 1878) created a huge autonomous Bulgaria and recognized the independence of Serbia, Montenegro and Romania; but the powers refused a Russian-made Balkans, and the Congress of Berlin, Bismarck as 'honest broker', cut Bulgaria in three, returned Macedonia to the sultan, gave Bosnia to Austria-Hungary's administration, and Cyprus to Britain. Russia had won the war and lost much of the peace.
para4: The wars' legacy was the modern Balkans and Russia's Black Sea position: Romania, Serbia, Montenegro and Bulgaria owed their independence substantially to Russian arms, while the Caucasus, Armenia's eastern lands and the fortress of Kars passed to the tsars. The two empires fought once more in the First World War, the disasters of Sarikamish and the Russian occupation of Erzurum and Trebizond, before both collapsed into revolution in 1917. The new Turkey that emerged from its own war of independence settled the last accounts with Russia's successor at the Straits and the Caucasus frontier, closing a rivalry that had lasted two and a half centuries.

title: The Concert of Europe
titleline: The Concert of Europe - The History Web
para1: The Concert of Europe was the informal system of great-power consultation that managed European affairs for a century, from the Congress of Vienna in 1815 to the First World War. It had no charter, no headquarters and no rules; it rested on two ideas: that the five great powers, Britain, Austria, Russia, Prussia and, from 1818, France, shared a common interest in preventing any one of them from dominating the continent, and that general war could be avoided if the powers met to settle dangerous questions together before fighting over them. The Vienna settlement itself, partitioning Europe by dynastic legitimacy and balance of power, was its founding act, and the Quadruple Alliance's congresses were meant to be its instrument.
para2: The early Concert worked through congress diplomacy: Aix-la-Chapelle (1818) admitted France to the club; Troppau, Laibach and Verona (1820-1822) quarreled over Austria's suppression of the Italian revolutions, driving Britain toward separation. The system bent but held through its first crises: Greek independence was managed jointly in 1827-1832 against the principle of legitimacy; Belgium's secession from the Netherlands (1830-1839) was negotiated into guaranteed neutrality; the Eastern crises of 1840 and 1878 were settled at London and Berlin without general war. Even the Crimean War (1853-1856), the Concert's worst failure, ended in a congress at Paris that readmitted the Ottoman Empire to the system.
para3: The mid-century wars of unification tested the Concert and, surprisingly, left its habit intact: Prussia's wars of 1864-1871 redrew the map without a general coalition forming against it, and Bismarck, having unified Germany, became the Concert's chief manager, his alliance system, the Congress of Berlin (1878), and the Mediterranean agreements all designed to localize conflicts and keep France isolated. After Bismarck's fall in 1890 the system's threads loosened: alliances hardened into the Triple Alliance and the Franco-Russian, then Anglo-French, blocs, imperial rivalries moved competition to Africa and Asia, and the arms race and war plans made mobilization schedules stronger than diplomacy.
para4: The Concert still scored late successes, the Algeciras Conference (1906) on Morocco, the London Conference (1912-1913) that drew Albania's borders after the Balkan Wars, but each success came at the price of entrenching the two armed camps. When the July Crisis of 1914 began, Austria-Hungary deliberately avoided the conference method that had defused earlier crises, Germany backed its ultimatums, Russia mobilized, and the alliance machinery the Concert had failed to replace pulled Europe into general war. The League of Nations, born in 1920, was in its way an attempt to give the Concert's idea, peace through consultation among powers, the permanent institutions it had always lacked.

title: The German Confederation
titleline: The German Confederation - The History Web
para1: Germany before unification was not a country but a civilization of states. The Holy Roman Empire had dissolved into, after 1648, some three hundred effectively sovereign principalities, duchies, bishoprics, free cities and knights' estates, the Kleinstaaterei that made Germany a patchwork of tolls, laws, armies and courts. The Empire provided a loose constitutional frame, the emperor, the Imperial Diet at Regensburg, imperial courts, but real power lay with the princes, above all the Habsburg emperors in Vienna and the Hohenzollern kings of Prussia, whose dualism dominated German history from 1740.
para2: Napoleon simplified the map by conquest. The mediatization of 1803 abolished most of the ecclesiastical states and folded the small territories into larger ones; the old Empire itself was dissolved in 1806, when a league of German princes formed the Confederation of the Rhine under French protection. The reforms of the era, Prussia's Stein and Hardenberg measures after the catastrophe of Jena (1806), Bavaria's and Baden's modernizations, created efficient centralized administrations, emancipated peasants and Jews to varying degrees, and, in the Wars of Liberation (1813-1815), awakened a German national consciousness that the restored princes refused to satisfy.
para3: The Congress of Vienna replaced the Empire with the German Confederation (Deutscher Bund), thirty-nine states under Austrian presidency with a diet at Frankfurt, deliberately too weak to act except in suppressing nationalism, Metternich's Carlsbad Decrees (1819) made that explicit. Economic integration outran politics: Prussia's Zollverein (customs union, 1834) bound most German states into a free-trade area that pointedly excluded Austria, making Prussia the economic leader of Germany a generation before it became the political one. The liberal and national movement of the Vormarz era, Burschenschaften and the Frankfurt Parliament of 1848, demanded unity and constitutions and was defeated, leaving unity to be achieved by state power instead.
para4: The path to unification ran through the rivalry of the two German great powers. Prussia under King William I and, from 1862, Bismarck built the army that would decide the German question, first taking Schleswig and Holstein from Denmark with Austria in 1864, then provoking the Austro-Prussian War of 1866: Koniggratz expelled Austria from German affairs, dissolved the Confederation, and let Prussia annex Hanover, Hesse-Kassel, Nassau and Frankfurt outright, founding the North German Confederation. The southern states were drawn in through the Franco-Prussian War (1870-1871), and on 18 January 1871 the German Empire was proclaimed in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles. The centuries of particularism ended in a federal empire dominated by Prussia.
source3label: Encyclopedia.com: Holy Roman Empire

title: The Deluge and the Swedish-Polish Wars
titleline: The Deluge and the Swedish-Polish Wars - The History Web
para1: The Polish-Swedish Wars were a long series of conflicts between the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth and Sweden, fought above all for control of the Baltic coast between 1563 and 1721. Their roots were both commercial, the customs wealth of Riga and the Vistula grain trade, and dynastic: Sigismund III Vasa, elected king of Poland in 1587, was also the hereditary heir of Sweden, and when his uncle seized the Swedish throne as Charles IX in 1600 and deposed him, Sigismund refused to renounce his claim. The resulting wars began in Livonia, where Swedish and Commonwealth armies fought over Estonia and Latvia through the 1620s: Gustavus Adolphus took Riga (1621) and most of Livonia, and from 1626 carried the war into Royal Prussia, where the Poles under Stanislaw Koniecpolski held him in check for three years.
para2: The truces that punctuated the fighting masked Sweden's gradual gain: by the Altmark Truce (1629) Sweden kept Livonia and the right to toll the Vistula ports, financing the army that Gustavus then led into Germany. The Commonwealth's eastern wars, against Cossacks, Russia and the Ottomans, gave Sweden its great opportunity. In 1655, while Poland reeled from the Khmelnytsky Uprising and the Russian invasion, Charles X Gustav attacked, and the Commonwealth nearly died: in the 'Deluge', the Swedish army overran and occupied most of the country by October 1655, and King John Casimir fled abroad. The occupation collapsed as Polish peasants and gentry rose against Swedish control, the defense of the Jasna Gora monastery at Czestochowa became the national legend, and by 1660 the Peace of Oliva ended the Deluge with Poland's sovereignty intact but exhausted.
para3: The last round came in the Great Northern War, when Augustus II the Strong, elector of Saxony and king of Poland, joined Russia and Denmark against Charles XII. The war devastated the Commonwealth: Charles deposed Augustus, imposed Stanislaus Leszczynski (1704), and used Poland as his base for the Russian campaign that ended at Poltava (1709). Augustus returned, but the Commonwealth had become a theater for other powers' armies and a protectorate of Russia, which guaranteed its 'Golden Liberty' constitution precisely because that constitution made the state ungovernable.
para4: The long wars with Sweden cost the Commonwealth its Baltic provinces, its best trade ports and, ultimately, its position as a great power: by 1721 Poland was financially broken, its army tiny, its liberum veto paralyzing reform, while Sweden too had spent its empire in the struggle. Both Baltic powers were eclipsed by Russia and Prussia, and when Poland was partitioned by its neighbors (1772-1795), Swedish interference was among the fatal weaknesses the partitioners exploited.
